blogs.title: "Click Cancelled": How Electronic Notices Meet Louisiana’s Strict Cancellation Statute
blogs.description: This post dissects why the Fifth Circuit found APAC’s e‑mail system satisfied every line of La. Rev. Stat § 9:3550(G)(3)(a), balancing statutory grammar with modern practice. We trace precedent from Delatte v Lemotte and Eaglin v Champion Ins., explain how courier‑style e‑mail fits the unelaborated “private carrier” term used in La.vinability, and consider what insurers nationwide can learn about migrating legacy paper workflows into automated APIs without risking pre‑cancellation litigation.

blogs.title: "Do You Need a Signature?" Separating Certifying Language from Formal Execution
blogs.description: Exploring one court’s refusal to obligate a signer under § 9 3550(G)(3)(a), this article reviews cases such as Benitez v Elsayed, Hodges v Colonial Lloyd’s Ins., and Lewis v Julien that tested whether a pleaded statement constitutes ‘certification’ absent a named employee’s signature. We evaluate why Judge Southwick concluded La.’s statutes allow uncertified copy‑certificatory notices, consider potential legislative reaction, and issue practical guidance for insurers designing electronic compliance packets.

blogs.title: "Receipt" Revisited: What It Means Under Louisiana Cancellation Law
blogs.description: Focusing exclusively on § 9 3550(G)(3)(b)(i), this post clarifies what ‘receipt’ buys an insurer when cancelling a financed policy. Drawing from Black’s Law Dictionary definitions used by the Fifth Circuit and analogies such as Huntley v Bayer MaterialScience, we outline why mere receipt by computer logs suffices while physical hand‑off does not mandate it, touch upon implications for other state statutes referencing receipt or possession, and highlight why certifying such an issue remains so elusive.

blogs.title: "Good Faith” Omitted Under Strict Adherence Doctrine
blogs.description: The court reaffirmed that once all statutory steps are performed—even if some seem perfunctory—the insurer cannot be held liable for good‑faith breach via summary judgment denial without ruling on procedural proof first. This analysis examines why plaintiffs’ insistence upon misrepresentation failed when governmental neutrality required strictly following contractual flow, discusses how this decision shapes future class actions against insurers using finance companies across France-St Louis zones, and warns attorneys who rely too heavily on implied good‑faith arguments absent explicit statutory violations.
